utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated to this rather early meeting at 9.00 mid-European summertime. Can we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I already ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom while I'll ask for the appearances. Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The schedule for today and for tomorrow is clear. I hope that we can continue this way. Mr. Koumjian, please, you wanted --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I was just going to alert the Registrar -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only that you know, having reviewed the transcript, I have to come back with some questions under Rule - I think it's - 96.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Further questions by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kuruzovic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we start, there was a long weekend in between. I just want to recall that you are always aware of your rights. First of all, I have to make it quite clear once again, you are not the accused in this case. You are here as a witness. You arrived without any subpoena. But nevertheless, you have the right to be assisted by counsel. You have the right to remain silent, also to remain silent on those questions where the answer could tend to be of self-incriminatory nature. And this right is an ongoing one. At any point in time, you may make use of this right. But let us go for a moment, please, in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's turn first to the question of the municipal -- the Serbian Municipal Assembly or as you called it the Serbian Assembly of the Municipality of Prijedor. On page 15, 16, of Day 143, you testified straightforward and without any hesitation that it was the 7th of January that the Serbian Assembly of the Municipality of Prijedor was formed, on the 7th of January. This is page 15 following lines 17 until page 16, line 4, Day 143. Then you told us the development until the 29th, when you had a meeting in the barracks. Then during the line of questions put to you by the Defence, being confronted with some documents, that in general, the name of the Assembly should be replaced and the word "Serbian" should appear. And a document showing that in a meeting, I think it was the fifth meeting of the Serbian Assembly, you were together with others elected; whereas in the beginning, you testified that you were already elected the 7th of January. Let me now hear first, what is, to the best of your recollection, the truth? Have you been already elected or maybe only provisionally elected already the 7th, or was it only Dr. Stakic and others, the president and vice-president, who were elected this 7th of December [sic], a remarkable day, the day of Orthodox Christmas. Can it be or may it be that during this meeting, mid-April 1992, the declaration or the election, as we can see it on the basis of the document, this is more or less a declaration, or was it only then that you yourself were elected?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've understood your question. I have been thinking while I was in the hotel, and I'm sure I must have made a mistake. As regards the establishment of the assembly, it took place on the 7th of January, and the president and the vice-president were elected on that day. And since this indeed was a remarkable day, I thought that everything was over on the 7th of January. But later on, there were ballots, and that was in mid-April. And on those ballots, the delegates voted for other people. I still have that ballot. I've remembered I've made a mistake, and I apologise once again for the mistake that I've made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then next question would be the 7th of January. This was apparently the first meeting. Mid-April, this was apparently the fifth meeting of this Serbian Assembly. Did you attend one of the meetings, the second, the third, or the fourth meeting of the Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having attended other meetings. But I must have remembered the one in April, and there's a good reason for that. At that time, I was doing my military obligation. That was in January. And in February, I was in Sarajevo sometime around the 2nd. I don't remember exactly when. Sometime around the 2nd, I got news that my daughter was ill, and that's when I went to Sarajevo with my daughter -- with my wife and my son. And I spent there almost a whole month while my daughter was awaiting surgery. And she has survived, thank God. And on the 4th March, I returned home from Sarajevo. So I really don't know when these sessions took place, and I don't remember having attended them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let's come to the second issue, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and this is the establishment of the Crisis Staff. I have to recall that straightforward and more than one hour, you testified on this, also the 143rd day of this case. You were asked: "When was the first meeting of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor?" My question, page 36, starting line 1 was: "Was it one, two, three, or five days after the takeover?" You said: "Perhaps three days. I don't recall exactly." And then on page 35, line 1, you stated: "It was two or three days after the takeover of power. I don't know who ordered this formation." And the same page, 35, line 22, I asked you: "When did you attend for the first time a meeting of the Crisis Staff"? You answered: "A few after the 30th of April. I can't remember exactly." Then later on, you were more concrete, told us that "The meetings were held in the basement of the Municipal Assembly where the canteen was," absolutely in line with the testimony of other witnesses. Then you went on, went on with the same testimony. I asked you on page 46, line 6: "It is correct that in conclusion with your previous testimony, this was more or less a declaration of that what already existed some days after the takeover? Would this be correct?" You answered: "Yes, yes." And then you continued on line 13: "Well, at that time the disposition was signed on the 17th that I was being relieved of my duty as the commander of the staff and was to attach myself to the brigade, to the army." So I think this simply confirms something that was already in existence and that it was simply legalised in this way because you know how it is with documents. They are always late. But this composition probably reflects what's there." This was when you were confronted with this document S180. Before I ask you, maybe it assists you that we for a moment listen what Mr. Miskovic has to tell us and told us in the past during the same reportage in Prijedor Municipality on this matter. Let me just see. This would be Document Number -- yes, once again, S91. You recall that we heard the clip when you gave an interview, but also Mr. Miskovic gave an interview that same day. Could the audiotape please be played now from that point where we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop. Here we can read "you are well aware and we have heard you are well aware of the events that ensued. However, as president of the party and the chairman of the Crisis Staff at that moment..." So Mr. Miskovic apparently speaks about the existence of a Crisis Staff already the 29th of April, 1992. How is this possible that when being asked by Mr. Lukic and being confronted with the document on the composition of the Crisis Staff and the establishment of the Crisis Staff in the Prijedor Municipality, you mentioned that "apparently I was wrong". It reads: "It was only the 20th of May." Previously when I confronted you with the same document, you state, as typical for paperwork, it's always late, and it was established already previously immediately after the takeover. Mr. Miskovic in this interview states that he was at that time or at that moment, to be more correct, the chairman of the Crisis Staff. Could you please try to explain us these different testimonies both from your side and from Mr. Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic liked to show off a bit, you know. Usually, he would introduce himself in the following way: Simo Miskovic -- just let me take a while to remember -- commander of the Crisis Staff for the Bosanska Krajina region. That's how he would always introduce himself. The staff that he was talking about, that was the party staff as the Crisis Staff of the SDS, the party. It was not a government staff, a government body. That was different, and this only came to being after two or perhaps three days after the takeover. That was later. These are two completely different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before you continue, may we hear Mr. Miskovic what he has to say later. Please continue with the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop. Stop. So you have heard that the Crisis Staff was mentioned twice related to the night from the 29th of April to the 30th of April. Once Mr. Miskovic stated: "Then I scheduled a meeting of the Crisis Staff for 2.00 a.m. and ordered Mr. Kuruzovic and Simo Drljaca to do the job with the army as we had agreed at the said meeting and that they were going to submit the report by 2.00 a.m." And then later on, after we have heard that immediately in the barracks, Mr. Kuruzovic, Mr. Kovacevic, and Stakic, Mr. Jankovic, Cado and others attended, and from the military side, Arsic and Zeka, then there was a discussion on the meeting, where to meet in the Hotel, and then finally at 2.00, I attended the session of the Crisis Staff and the reports were submitted and it was decided by the Crisis Staff that the takeover will commence at 4.00 hours a.m. and that's how it started." Could you please comment on this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is about what he called Crisis Staff, but that's the party Crisis Staff because he was the president of the municipal board of the SDS. The rest of it is correct and truthful. As far as the military aspect is concerned, which refers to me, there was no special army there because I was the commander of the regional staff of the Territorial Defence at that time, and we simply informed the people who were outside the town across the local communes that should there be any shooting or any major problems arising, they should be prepared to defend the people. As for the other part concerning the takeover, that was carried out by the police in its entirety, and that was organised by Simo Drljaca, Jankovic, Cadzo, Marko Dzenadija and so on and so forth. So if you want me to repeat this, this is not the same Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, so when was this SDS as you call it, SDS Crisis Staff, when was this Crisis Staff established?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know. I was not aware of the existence of any such thing officially. But Simo knows this. I told you that in March, I was not in Prijedor at all. Whether the party set this up earlier on someone's orders and on whose orders, well, yeah, I should assume so. As far as I remember, there was a Crisis Staff, and there was the imminent threat of war that had been proclaimed on the level of the whole party. So he said that this should be official. I'm sorry to say this, but I think he was merely showing off, even what we just heard, the interview. He was a show-off in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But it is still your testimony that at that time, something else existed, and this would be the SDS Crisis Staff. Correct? Opposed to the Crisis Staff established then later based on the documents both me and later Mr. Lukic has shown to you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The election, the voting at the assembly, that's when this one was set up. The Executive Board and the president of the Assembly, that was there. And as soon as the takeover occurred two or three days later, I can't remember accurately, then someone ordered someone from the Krajina, Autonomous Region, I suppose, Karadzic probably, said that Crisis Staffs should be established from the Executive Boards and said who the members should be of these Crisis Staffs. Whether this was actually ordered by the president of the republic or the presidency or the Crisis Staff of the Krajina Autonomous Region from Banja Luka, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then to be quite concrete, when it reads here, there was a meeting, and this is absolutely in line with what you told us beforehand, "I went up to the barracks where Kuruzovic, Mico Kovacevic, and Stakic, Simo Jankovic, Cadzo and others were," what was this? Was this a meeting of the SDS Crisis Staff or was it a meeting of that what was called by others shadow government or option 2, that what was elected mid-April 1992? Was it already a meeting of those people who should form the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serbian Municipal Assembly as of the takeover, recall the document shown to you by Mr. Koumjian, that it was ordinary in the past planned for the 1st of May, and then a decision was taken to implement this already the -- during the night from the 29th to the 30th of April? So what was this meeting in the barracks, a meeting of the upcoming Municipal Assembly and those persons replacing others in the municipality, or was it a meeting of the SDS Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably a mix between the two. This was not a wholly official body. I was then the commander of the regional staff in Urije and Prijedor too, so that's probably why they wanted me to be there, too. Only later when I remember, when I thought about April, the proposal, the municipal elections for commander. This was a meeting of a group of people, certainly party representatives, who when Mr. Stakic found out about the telegram and brought it there and when it was read out, as I said, I did not hear it in its entirety. A while before Mr. Miskovic came, I arrived, too, but I understood -- because there was no reason for me to believe it wasn't that way, but now I've had an opportunity to actually see and become familiar with the content of that document, and a decision was taken and an agreement was reached there. About what later happened at 4.00 in the morning, when the police, in an organised manner, left and took over the facilities. And then at 6.00, the officials went to their positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, did you attend a meeting of the SDS Crisis Staff prior to the 29th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember. I had not even heard up to that point that it was referred to as the Crisis Staff. I don't remember attending any such meetings. And it was a long time ago. I think not, but I can't be positive about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this assisting which indeed helped to clarify things a little bit more. Let me now come to the third point and let us hear what Dr. Stakic has to say on this. May we please play Exhibit Number S187. This is a video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop. Stop. Is this assessment of Dr. Stakic correct, that Trnopolje was mainly filled with Muslims from Kozarac, a good part of those extremists were from Kozarac and they went to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This first part of Mr. Stakic's statement is true, most of those people were from Kozarac. As for the latter part of his statement, I don't know they were extremists or not. There were many men there who were military -- who were fit for military service, able-bodied men. I don't know the exact figures, but what he started saying when you interrupted the tape, 1.450, I'm not how many of them UNHCR later took to Karlovac. I don't know whether those men were healthy and able-bodied, whether they were extremists or not, but no one there acted in such a way as to create any special problems apart from the difficult conditions themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But can you understand why Dr. Stakic used the terms "Muslims" and "part of those being extremists"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the people we referred to as Muslims, probably he believed that among those people, there were men who were extremists. Now why and what grounds, I really don't know. Probably on the basis of something that happened later. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be true that as it is stated here: "Trnopolje was mainly filled with Muslims from Kozarac"? Would this be true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, later people came from the town. They arrived by train, by cars, in cars from Hambarine. But most of them were from Kozarac, or at least I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then in order to save time, if you want, we can play also this part of the one and same interview. Previously Dr. Stakic said: "These places such as Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje, were a necessity in a given moment and were formed according to a decision of the civilian authorities in Prijedor. "Reporter: So these three camps, or how are they -- Dr. Stakic: Reception centres. Reporter: "Reception centre, they were formed according to a decision of your civilian authorities. Stakic: Yes, yes." To be continued. Who were those civilian authorities in Prijedor taking the decision to establish Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the latter two, I don't know, I can only assume about Trnopolje. I told you how it was established. If there was an agreement or a decision, I was not aware of it. I was simply surprised, and there was that request that was made, and I did say that. Whether the other thing was necessary, too, I don't know. Those were investigation services as far as I knew. Only the public security centre had the authority to establish those on the orders of someone from the government or the Ministry of the Interior. Now, whether there was any agreement with the municipal leaders from other segments, I really don't know, believe me. I can only speak about Trnopolje. Whatever else I said, I simply stated what I believed. If there were extremists, if it was necessary to look into their actions, for them to give statements, then that's what it was for. But Trnopolje was not a camp; it was something quite different. It was a gathering of unfortunate people at the time, a refuge for people to go to, as we called it. People fled from combat operations to save their necks, elderly people, women, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown the document tendered by the Defence, 65 ter number 414. Once again, the English version, please, on the ELMO and B/C/S to the witness. Would this be correct that this is a, as we can read at the top of the page, a decision or a document issued by the 1st Krajina Corps command, confidential number 621, from 2 September, 1992? And then please look what we can see under number 2. And would you please be so kind and read in B/C/S the entire number 2.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The following was agreed in reference to the closure of Manjaca and Trnopolje prisoner of war camps. First, to evacuate 79 sick detainees from the Manjaca and Trnopolje camps; to secure their unobstructed transport to the Mahovljani airport in Banja Luka; on that day, to open the airport for the landing of ICRC aircraft that would transport the sick prisoners of war abroad for treatment. "After their requests have been met and we accepted our obligations, they were advised to seek authorisation from the Croatian authorities for landing the aircraft because Mahovljani airport was under Croatian fire. "Taking note of this, they gave a clear commitment to notify us about the operation of transporting prisoners of war at least 24 hours before so that could secure the landing and take-off of the aircraft. At this point, they handed us a list of names of 65 prisoners of war who are either wanted or ill."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop. You can see that the 1st Krajina Corps command apparently used totally different terms. It started already: "The following was agreed in reference to the closure of Manjaca and Trnopolje prisoners of war camps." And it ends, quoting a list of the names of 65 prisoners of war. Then let's please continue. May the usher please show the Defence exhibit tendered by the Defence, 65 ter number 416. Once again, issued by the 1st Krajina Corps command, operational confidential number 655, 11 September, 1992. "Decision on granting amnesty from criminal prosecution. Article 1, the following prisoners of war in Manjaca and Trnopolje prisons are freed from criminal prosecution." And then it follows a list of 69 detainees. So once again, prisoners of war in Trnopolje prison. Could you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. please explain how it's possible that the 1st Krajina Corps command comes to a totally different assessment of what Trnopolje was at that time. Was it a prison as reflected in the last document? Was it a prisoner of war camp? And that there were prisoners of war in this camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where these names come from. I don't know what these -- who these people are. Maybe they are from Manjaca. I don't know. I've already said on several occasions that this name does not correspond to what Trnopolje was. And anybody who was there can confirm that. Regardless of how long they spent there, no Muslim was in uniform there, and I didn't see any Muslims arriving with weapons there. So I really don't know who the people referred to in this document are. I don't remember anybody leaving in this way from Trnopolje. I remember that only once the UNHCR came. I don't know when that was. I don't know exactly. It may have been in June or in July. I don't know exactly. And some 30 or 40 men were on their list. It was said that they were sick and that they were supposed to be transported by plane to London for treatment. I believe that the deputy minister of health also came, and they were checked by a doctor from Prijedor. I didn't interfere with all that because I didn't know who these people are and on what grounds they were taken away. But I believe that that was that one occasion when some of the people left. As for the fact that they were prisoners of war, that is out of the question, and I can swear before God and I can claim that Trnopolje was not even a camp, let alone a prison as it is stated herein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You can see that the latter document, it reads: "We received the following telegram from the presidency of the Serbian Republic," and then it starts with a quote, and it's finally signed by the president of the Presidency, Dr. Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in his assessment apparently, it was granting amnesty in relation to Trnopolje prisons. And the other documents, speaking the same language "prisoner of war camps" and once again, "65 prisoners of war." So how can we bring your testimony together with the other testimony? Was it maybe a mix? Was there a separate unit within Trnopolje which could be called a, as it reads here, "prisoner of war camp" or, in the other document, "prison"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Trnopolje was never any such thing. There were -- people were never interrogated there. There were no investigations carried out there, so I really don't know understand what this is all about. Was there maybe some other private agreement, I really don't know. I can see here that this was signed by the president. I see the term "prisoners of war". I see that both Manjaca and Trnopolje are being referred to as prisons. It doesn't say here how many of these people were in Trnopolje, among those who were taken away. I really don't remember. I just told you that at the very beginning, some people were indeed taken away from Trnopolje by somebody who came from the ministry. And they had a list on which it said that these people were sick and that they were being transported to London for treatment. That's the way I understood it. I could not influence that. I could not have a bearing on that, whether they would go or not go. There was a list signed by the Red Cross. I suppose the Red Cross was aware of that. I believe that there must have been a preliminary agreement with either the Red Cross or the UNHCR. Their representatives were in Trnopolje on a daily basis, and they themselves could see that this was not a camp or a prison, that people were not being brought in or taken away. If somebody had been a prisoner, they would have been tied, I suppose, but something like that never happened in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know Colonel Milutin Vukelic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukelic, no, never heard of him. I can see here that that was signed by him in the corps command, but I don't know who that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But I hope, Mr. Kuruzovic, that based on these documents and Dr. Stakic's own comments, we have some doubts on your testimony on the nature of Trnopolje. And maybe following now and answering the questions put to you by Mr. Koumjian, maybe it will assist you and maybe there will be a chance and a possibility for you to correct, in whole or in part, your previous testimony. Because I think you can agree that on the basis of these documents, a totally different impression is given of that what is the nature of Trnopolje. Would you agree? Would you please --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a big surprise for me. I've never heard any such thing. I've never seen any such thing. I don't know why Trnopolje would be made equal to Manjaca or some other camp. I don't know on what grounds. Maybe this was just a matter of red tape or administration. Maybe -- given the fact that people were gathered in several places, one term was given to all of these places just to facilitate things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you agree that the list of names you can read here, the 69 names, that these are Muslim names?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read all of them, but I can see this guy, his name is Milomir Antunovic, he is not a Muslim. But the majority are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Which was the number you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 58. Number 9 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Milomir Antunovic. Do you know him in person?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I can tell by the first name and by the last name that he cannot be a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the same would be true of number 9, Janko Antunovic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be honest, for us it's extremely difficult to make a distinction between Muslims, Serbs, Croats, based on the name. In the past, we were never acquainted to do this exercise, but unfortunately in this period of time, we have to look very seriously on the question of the ethnic background of these persons. I hope we can overcome this distinction we have made in the past in the future. For the moment, it remains for me only to do some technical exercise, and this would mean Document 65 ter number 414 was tendered by the Defence. Are there any objections by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then it would be admitted into evidence as D126A and B correspondingly. And the other, 65 ter 416, the document from the 11th of September, 1992, this would be D127A and B correspondingly. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Both documents are --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Both documents are admitted into evidence under these numbers. May I then ask, please, Mr. Koumjian, to continue with your line of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, you've mentioned several times the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Did any leaders of the Autonomous Region of Krajina such as Radoslav Brdjanin or Dr. Vukic or the mayor Predrag Radic visit the Trnopolje camp, the Trnopolje reception centre, whatever name you want to use for it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As for Brdjanin and who else, Predrag Radic, they were never there. And as for Vukelic, he's a doctor, no, I don't think so. I don't remember. I don't remember their names. But if they had been, they would have probably come together. Brdjanin, Radic were certainly not there. And as for Dr. Vukelic, I think that he wasn't there either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's Dr. Vukic who I believe was the SDS president in Banja Luka, just to we're clear we're talking about the same person. You never saw a Dr. Vukic to your knowledge did not visit the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How about Stojan Zupljanin or General Talic, did you ever see them at the camp? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you aware of a visit by Mr. Brdjanin and Predrag Radic and others from Banja Luka, Stojan Zupljanin, to Prijedor in July?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. They may have been there, but I don't remember. If they had been there, they probably talked to the president of the municipality and the president of the Executive Board, not with me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about the Crisis Staff of the SDS. To your knowledge, who were the members of the SDS Crisis Staff that existed prior to the takeover?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, I heard that only subsequently. These are the terms that Mr. Miskovic used. I was not in Prijedor at that time. But if there had been such a Crisis Staff, then its members should have been members of the presidency of the Serbian Democratic Party of Prijedor. As far as I can see, Mr. Simo Miskovic is talking about the party Crisis Staff at the time when this happened. This was before the war, during the imminent threat of war. I don't know what else to call that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say the presidency of the SDS party in Prijedor, do you mean the president and the vice-president of the party for Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, president, vice-president, and probably some other people who were presidents of various standing committees and who helped with the work. And if there had been a Crisis Staff, then nobody else but these people could be its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You were asked some questions by Mr. Lukic about Dr. Stakic, Dr. Stakic's party membership. It was clear in 1991 that Dr. Stakic was a member of the SDS, and in fact, he was the vice-president of the party. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was the vice-president of the party. I know he was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly. I hear -- I heard it only the other day that he was not a member of the SDS, but it is quite possible. Later on, he was. I know that for a fact, when he was the president of the Municipal Assembly. Whether he was even before that, really, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown S94, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just while that's being prepared, sir, what kind of car did you drive when you were working at the Trnopolje camp? Excuse me, Trnopolje centre.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Renault given to me by the company called Borac from Prijedor, and I returned it after only a few days. And I returned it because a guy called Icic offered me to take a car that was in his garage. He took me there, gave me the keys. This car was a Golf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry, what was the name of the gentleman that gave you his car?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his name was Icic, Fikret or something like that. Yes. And that car was then registered there and mobilised. And when I was demobilised on the 22nd August, 1993, that car was given to the brigade command, and I believe that the brigade command then gave it to the hospital. I believe that was the sequence of events with this car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, why did Mr. Fikret Icic give you his car to use?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was afraid that somebody else would take it, so nobody would know where that car was because such things happened. And if you remember, we were talking about the establishment -- actually, whether the Municipal Assembly was supposed to issue orders to the army and to the police to control these cars which were driven without a travel order. Unfortunately, a number of people from my ethnic group confiscated property from other people. This man offered me the car because he knew I would look after it, and once everything was rectified and once I was demobilised, that car would be returned to him. So that I believe if he really went there to ask for the car, that the car had indeed been returned to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was Mr. Icic in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, now, in front of you is S94.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his name was. Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We're now turning to S94. You'll see that these are some notes from the minutes -- excuse me, minutes of the assembly meeting of the Prijedor SDS party held on the 11th of September, 1991. There's an interjection, page 3 of the English. Sorry, I don't have the B/C/S in front of me. By someone named Kuruzovic. Sir, do you believe that that would be you, the person who indicated objected to Article 44, moving that the text "but must be a member of the SDS BH be included." Would that be you? Would that indicate to you that you were in attendance at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this is my name, it could only be me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, do you see that in this document, there were elections for the party president and for the party vice-president. And that 139 individuals voted in the election for the vice-president, Milomir Stakic received 103 of the 139 votes. Does this remind you that Dr. Stakic was the vice-president of the SDS party as of the 11th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it. But if this is how it reads, then it must be true. I've located that. It says vice-president, Dragan Savanovic, Milomir Stakic, 103. And some Mirko Galamdzija or whatever his name is, 7 votes. So that means that Dr. Stakic became the vice-president of the party. I said that I knew that he was an SDS member, but I don't know at what period of time, from when up to when.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like the usher to please distribute another document that has not been entered into evidence. It's 65 ter 316 on the Prosecution 65 ter list. It has the ERN number in English beginning 03015836.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You had testified, sir, about receiving a uniform. You said that was intended for Mr. Srdic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was told. I was told that there was no uniform for me. Later on, I signed the receipt of that uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, according to your testimony, as I understand it, conflict broke out in Prijedor after the 22nd of May. Is that correct? Sometime after the Hambarine incident.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you can take a look at this document, and perhaps the first page of the English could be put on the ELMO, or has it already? Thank you. And I believe Your Honours has copies. Do you see that it indicates that the Prijedor Municipal Assembly acquired a certain quantity of material for sewing flags and green camouflage uniforms according to a delivery note dated the 3rd of May, 1992. And that the ordered goods were received on the 28th of May, 1992. Would this indicate to you, sir, that uniforms that were made for members of the Crisis Staff and others of prominence were ordered just after the takeover of power?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. If this is official, then I assume the answer would be yes. As far as I know, the uniform that I received and those who were members of the Crisis Staff, those uniforms were not green. They were light-brown with some yellow patches or spots. It was a very lightweight summer uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It was camouflage, when you say "spots"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I can tell you that this type of uniform was worn by every single manager of every company in town. Nobody forced them to wear those uniforms, but what do I know? Maybe they wanted to go with the flow. All managers wore such uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have another document I would like distributed. And that is -- has the ERN number 03074605 in English. It begins with that, and concludes with 03074610A. And the B/C/S begins P, as in Paul, 0008404, through 8410.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not to lose control on the documents, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. previous one would be provisionally marked S432A and B respectively. And the now distributed would be S433A and B respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, this latest document is one of those I asked you to look at over the weekend. Perhaps before we begin with that and so I don't forget, I also asked you to look over that newspaper article that was marked S238, Kozarski Vjesnik. Excuse me, that's not the right number. I asked you to look over a newspaper article that we discussed yesterday -- Friday. And that was an interview with you from 1995. Was there anything else in that article -- or was there anything in the article that you wanted to comment on or dispute, the 1995 article?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd prefer a more straightforward question if that's possible. This was a piece of coverage on the memorial day, the day when the takeover took place. I may have been trying to show off a little bit there myself. You know, everyone likes people to talk about them -- everyone likes people to see them as able persons. But I suppose I am about to receive some more specific questions from you regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm trying to be specific. Is there anything false in that newspaper article?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are several things there that were not mentioned and are connected to this. This Mr. Grubor who came to request, well, -- the way is seems here is that he was under my command, that he had - I don't know how many people - both armed and unarmed. So perhaps I should clarify that a little bit. At that time, there was a war in Slovenia. I'd already returned home. I'd buried my daughter. But in 1991, in late September or early October, at the request of the people, a meeting was held at the local commune building in Prijedor. About a thousand people were there. A decision was made, which had been requested by the representatives of all parties. But that was not a party meeting for people to be listed, to draw up lists of people, people who were members of the JNA, because they believed that that was the only form of protection because all sorts of things were happening about town already and people were scared. So people signed up who were members of the TO and the police, too. Even those who had been members of the brigades, and sometimes not. They wanted to be counted on should there be an attack against the Serbian people. There were even women there, young men, young women. That's what it was about. And there were TO men there who were armed. They probably thought that that was some sort of an army or some armed group. And this gentleman came there requesting -- well, you can imagine what it looked like if I released any lists to him. Anyway, I was not the one keeping the lists. Stevanovic was, what's his name? This is something that was public. As far as I remember, about 4.000 people signed up, women, young men, girls. So perhaps I could answer the question why this sort of thing happened. At that time, the 343rd Brigade was on the front in Western Slavonia, the 5th Kozara, the 6th Sana, and the 11th Dubica Brigade, including a lot of people from Prijedor, mostly Serbs, but there were Muslims there, Croats, throughout the war even at the commands of these brigades, Muslim citizens, Croatian citizens. And most of the Muslims who had served their military service were in Prijedor. It was the talk of the town how Muslims were arming themselves. And some of them were members of the reserve police forces, people were scared because a lot of men had left town. And these remained. So that was a thing that happened of its own volition, simultaneously. That's how it happened. So he thought in the spring that this still existed and he was requesting people and that kind of thing and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the record, I believe it's time for a break. But the document we were talking about, the one you read over the weekend was the one entitled "memories of April's events in 1992" and that was S430, just for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Does Your Honour wish to take a break now before we begin with the next document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have to stay with this document for only one purpose. If you could please be so kind and have a look on the fifth-last paragraph, that's in English, the English version page 5, and there it's the fourth paragraph where it reads: "At the meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor and the Garrison command held on 10th of June, 1992, and attended by Major Slobodan Kuruzovic" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I actually haven't begun. He was talking about the last document on Friday. It's my fault for confusing the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Of course. Then let's come back to this. It's then for you. The trial stays adjourned until 5 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Now once again, sorry that I already anticipated something you want to discuss. But please, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, could you please explain to us what your role was in the logistics base at Cirkin Polje, and explain how it changed, if it did, over time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, it was a TO staff. Until the brigade commander's order came on the resubordination, and then the order was confirmed from the administration of the Municipal Assembly. There was a decision. And as I said, one of the main tasks was to provide food for all checkpoints throughout the municipal territory. After the 16th or the 17th, I can't remember the date, after that order, the staff was abolished, and it was transformed into a so-called logistics base which continued to work on the same tasks, providing food to all checkpoints, and then regional staffs in the whole town, or rather in the whole municipality, down to Ljubija, Brezicani, on to Omarska. That's where another regional TO staff was. It was all TO. And the army and the police, they all got their supplies from there. Later, the chief of the logistics base was Mirko Mudrinic. I only occasional used the opportunity on my way to Trnopolje, because it was necessary for the children, and they would give me milk and fruit, fruit juice, bread, from the Zitopromet company and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So please explain, after the Territorial Defence was absorbed into the army, into the 43rd Brigade, by the order of Colonel Arsic and the order of the Crisis Staff of the 29th of May, signed by Dr. Stakic, did you continue to have any role in the Cirkin Polje logistics base other than stopping by to pick up food for children?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any particular role. I was not in a leading role of any kind certainly. Those other people who remained at the base were in charge. As far as the fuel supplies and the fuel distribution and the certificates was concerned, the municipal organ was in charge of that. I don't think it was even the logistics base. That's what I'd been in charge of, right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused when you say you didn't have any particular role or a leading role. Did you have any road in the logistics base, let's say, from June on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said what I did. I would sometimes use the opportunity for them to give me and they did give me very often food, milk, cigarettes, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: These are things for yourself, these are things for the persons in Trnopolje? Who was -- for the guards at Trnopolje? Who did you get these things for?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the guards and for the people. Among those who came with their unit commanders, there were no women and children. At the Red Cross, there were. It was because of the small children. Because the children, there were lots of small children in the camp. The cigarettes Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were for the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And this is items that you would carry yourself to the camp, to Trnopolje? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I put it into the boot of my car, and when I arrived, I would distribute it to the guards and to the people. But the people knew that I would always bring something, apples, milk, other kinds of fruit. Elderly people, Muslims, would be waiting for me most often in the morning when I arrived, and then they would take these things to the children over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, did you originally -- your original work with the logistics base, in addition to food, part of your duties were to issue these certificates for fuel. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was right at the beginning. Before the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly regulated the whole thing in a different way, and then it was done by a kiosk which was close to the logistics base, and then the municipal officials were in charge of issuing those certificates after that. Whatever was left, they took from us. The lists, the records. As to how many certificates had been issued, to which persons, to which companies, and then all the companies got their fuel from there. Some of those companies, that is, the car that they gave over there, they used them for their own needs. So when food was being taken or water to the checkpoints, there were cars and companies would be going and then come back the next morning and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Originally, were you based in the Municipal Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was at the logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps you could explain, on the transcript for the Day 143, that is, your testimony Wednesday, on page 19 of my LiveNote -- I notice my page numbers are never the same as Mr. Lukic's for some reason, line 7, you stated: "It was the Executive Board, the Executive Board which urged us to move out of the municipal hall and to undertake to issue - I mean the Territorial Defence staff - to issue vouchers to issue fuel, petrol vouchers, petrol coupons there so that companies and self-employed entrepreneurs, those who needed fuel, that to go there to be issued with some kind of voucher so they could get fuel." So can you explain why you said on Wednesday that you were urged by the Executive Board to move out of the municipal building, municipal hall? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you misunderstood me. They asked for that job not to be done at the municipality building because that was an admin building. All the services serving citizens in any way since the takeover were there, so that would create a mess. So they wanted this to be done at the -- wherever the logistic base was. But this only lasted for about 10 days. I can't remember exactly. And then the Municipal Assembly service took over. They had set up a kiosk there, and that's where this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are you saying that you never worked -- the Territorial Defence staff never worked out of the municipal hall?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, never, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, where did you get the fuel from that you issue the vouchers for? There was not a refinery, I presume, in Prijedor. Where did the fuel come from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not getting fuel. The fuel was being sold. Fuel in Prijedor was stored in Jugopetrol or Krajinapetrol, I can't remember exactly. The distance between the town was 6 kilometres, and this was their own service area or rather station, and they were selling it. The Municipal Assembly probably influenced the fact that not anyone was in a position to get as much as they would like. So a voucher would be issued and they would go there and get fuel from that petrol station. But not in unlimited quantities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You've anticipated my next question. What guidelines did you receive as to who to give the vouchers to or the quantities allowed? Were you allowed to give the vouchers just to your friends as much as they wanted, or did you receive some guidelines, some rules, about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no special guidelines as to how much. Someone might have private needs, someone may have been ill, so these people would be given about 5 litres. If it was a more remote part of town, it would have been 10. And then companies could take up to 50, talking about oil. I hope that I did my job in an honest way. I did have complaints coming in from the municipal officials who thought that I would just let it go and let people have as much as they thought they needed, so they complained with the president of the Executive Board and the president of the municipality. They wanted me not to give away so much fuel. So that may have been one of the reasons why the municipal officials took over the job at a later stage. I may have made a mistake at some point and given someone 7 instead of 5 litres because the person had special reasons for needing fuel, but I don't remember that. Maybe there were such cases, exceptionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you provide fuel to the army and the police so that -- to ensure that they had sufficient fuel for their needs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And this was -- you were issuing these again at the -- under the authority of the Executive Board or Municipal Assembly? They're the ones that authorised you to issue the certificates. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the army and the police came with orders from the brigade commander stating -- or the secretariat of the interior. But not so often the secretariats. I think they got their fuel from the army and a certificate would be issued. Most of it was for the medical centre, because many people had to go to Banja Luka for kidney operations and dialysis. So every morning, there would be a person who was taking them there in all the ambulances for all the hospitals and the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's go to the report on mobilised motor vehicles in Cirkin Polje logistics base. That's in front of you dated the 17th of June. Sir, I'm a bit confused when you indicate that you had no role in the logistics base from June on when apparently this document indicates that you attended a meeting regarding the logistics base. I'm looking at page 9 of the English. On page 9 of the English, I don't have the B/C/S in front of me, but it would be -- it has the date the 10th of June, and it should be the fifth paragraph from the end. Excuse me, I have the draft, and Ms. Karper has given me the final. I may have the wrong numbers. If you see the signature of Mr. Mudrinic, if you go up six paragraphs from the end, so six paragraphs from the end --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, we would like to follow you. Our English version ends on page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I was using a draft that we had last week, and Ms. Karper just gave it to me. So the English is now page 5. Thank you. And on the B/C/S, it would be the page ending 8408, the second paragraph on that page, the first full paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In that paragraph it states that "at the meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor and the garrison command held on the 10th of June, 1992, and attended by Major Slobodan Kuruzovic, commander of the Serbian army staff as well as deputy commander for logistics, Mirko Mudrinic, and then also quartermaster Stevan Nikolic and all commanders of sector staffs, all instructions given by the garrison command and the Crisis Staff relating to the transformation of the Territorial Defence into the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were accepted." Do you recall this meeting of the Crisis Staff and garrison command held on the 10th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. But probably it was held, and it says that I was in attendance. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you explain in what role you would have attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, as you can see, is the 17th of June, the time when the staff comes into existence. And this report dates to the beginning of the existence of a part of the logistics base. So this is a working report, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cars that were mobilised on the 2nd and 3rd of May. There are a number of those that were mobilised later when I was no longer there but I was supposed to attend because there were reports which pertained to the period when I was there at the staff. Regardless of whether I was a member or not, it was my duty to be there and to confirm what they wrote here in this report. Among other things, they discussed about the transition of the Territorial Defence as a whole to the army of Republika Srpska. I am not only referring to the Serbian TO, the TO in its entirety. But you know what the times were like. There was a special name, but actually it was all the same because at that time, there were only Serbs that were members of the TO, except at the command. At the command, there were Muslims, and that other part over there in the town, there were also Muslims but that was a little bit divided already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The report indicates, if we go up a few paragraphs, going up two paragraphs: "We would like to point out that from the day of the takeover and the establishment of the logistics section in the Serbian army TO staff in Prijedor, up to the 10th of June, in addition to many sanitation and medical measures, we have also provided the weapons and ammunition for sector staffs and secured and delivered about a hundred thousand meals to members of the police and Serbian army TO units." So was part of the duties of the logistics base to also distribute weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not weapons, ammunition. The weapons, they had. I said the TO, which was part of the town, but when there was the takeover, then everything was all the same thing, it was more under the command of Mr. Javoric than mine because anyway, I did not have any special military units. But this all went together, and I was in a lot of difficulty issuing certificates for fuel and all the other miracles. And then all the way until the incident that happened there, and then I had to go to Trnopolje. But, for example, this would be given to the police, the army units because you see they're referring to the TO and the Serbian army, too, because when the Serbian army existed, then there was no more TO. And the man who wrote this report -- well, you do understand what it's about. The food, the ammunition, and all of that. This was given all at once because as far as I remember, aside from that, it wasn't used very much because there were no ongoing operations in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was it the Crisis Staff that directed the logistics support from this base?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that the logistics base had, the orders had to be given from the secretary for the economy. For example, if somebody was to take bread, then an approval had to be given. And as far as I know, reports had to be written on the quantities of food that were taken. At the beginning, this was taken from a restaurant in town, and the food was taken to the checkpoints. Thereafter, this was prepared in the logistics base, and it was transported either by lorries or by cars, depending on how far away the checkpoints where the food was needed were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, if we go up one paragraph, and that would be in English the bottom of page 4, it begins: "Since 1st of May, 1992, Cirkin Polje logistics base has been providing complete logistics support to all police officers in Centar, Prijedor II, and all members of" and it lists a number of local sector staffs. "Supplies have been delivered in accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor on the basis of which a report has been compiled and sent to the Crisis Staff and garrison command." And I believe that's consistent with what you just told us. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, reports so that it was known what was given to the military, how much food, how much of everything else, and the same applied to all the Territorial Defence, all the regional staffs across the town, and that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going back to the paragraph I began with, that's page 5, that begins: "At the meeting of the Crisis Staff held on 10 June, 1992... ," is it correct, sir, that the logistics centre also provided food to the Keraterm and Omarska prisons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, but I don't know whether it was transported for here or was it the police that transported it? But whatever was within the purview of either the police or the army, the food was prepared there and transported from there. I don't know that the food would be taken from this logistic base to Omarska and Keraterm. I believe that this was first taken to the police, and then the police distributed it and transported it. But I can't be sure, I can't claim that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we could now have -- Ms. Karper prepared 65 ter 368.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Are you ready to leave this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm ready to leave this document if Your Honour has some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then please, in the same paragraph you just mentioned, it was said you participated in the meeting of the 10th of June. I already confronted you previously with the enactments passed this 10th of June, 1992, based on the document S250, and only to recall the first conclusion was requesting the municipal secretariat to report on the logistics base. Second, assigning the duty of providing security for the Trnopolje camp to the regional command. Would it be correct to conclude that you in fact participated in this meeting of the Crisis Staff the 10th of June, and you were present when these two issues were dealt with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that I did, since this is what it says here. But not as a member of the Crisis Staff. This report covered a longer period of over a month. I was supposed to attend this meeting as somebody who had participated in the reorganisation of these tasks relative to the supply of food to the army and the police, the checkpoints, the supply of fuel and so on and so forth. Because here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's absolutely in line with that what we can read in Document S250. There was, for example, an order banning Krajina petrol company from issuing petrol without Crisis Staff permits. This would fall under your area - Correct? - of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I issued those permits or certificates and then people would go buy fuel. The Executive Board demanded a maximum savings or -- of energy and fuel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then that we are not once again confusing the months, it's not a document of May 1992, but the document dated the 17th of June. And here it reads: "The decision" - in the first paragraph - "the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor, and the orders of the commander of the Serbian army Territorial Defence staff of Prijedor Municipality, Major Slobodan Kuruzovic. Troops and equipment were mobilised in the logistical support staff." That would mean that, in fact, this 17th of June, 1992, you still were the commander of the Serbian army Territorial Defence staff of Prijedor Municipality. Correct, as it reads in paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. This is a report which was written on the 17th and covered everything that happened up to that date, including the things relative to the Territorial Defence staff, and the logistics base. Some of these cars were mobilised at the very beginning, and most of the people were drivers from these companies who would work in their companies in the afternoon, and then work other things in the morning. So this is submitted by Mudrinic, the chief of the logistics base. But whatever was carried over to that base prior to the 17th of June, I don't know whether anything else is mentioned here, so everything that was carried over up to the 17th of June, together in the logistics base and the territorial staff. I never submitted these reports before. I hope I've helped you to understand this. So this is a report that covers a long period. I can see the dates here, the 2nd of May, the 3rd of May, and after the 17th -- actually, the 29th, I no longer operated in the capacity of a commander of the staff, of the territorial staff, as per the decision that we saw. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So repeat, you do not dispute that you attended the meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor and the garrison command held on 10th of June, 1992, and attended by Major Slobodan Kuruzovic, commander of the Serbian army staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is just the way he put it, because later on, I did not have any position or post. And prior to that, I had that one. I was in the brigade. It was just a habit. He had to mention some position that I had, but not the one that I had at that time, but the one that I had prior to that because he mentions things happening on the 2nd and the 3rd of May. So this is a report that covers a month and a half period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then we have also a prologue in an addendum to the report. And there it reads: "On 15th of June, 1992, a number of members of the Territorial Defence staff of the Serbian army, members of Cirkin Polje logistics bases who are permanently involved in the securing of Trnopolje refugee centre addressed a request to the leadership of the command logistic base underscoring the problem of fuel shortage" and so on and so forth. And then under 5, it reads: "Slobodan Kuruzovic took a diesel vehicle, Golf vehicle, registration number PD-630-02 from Fikret Icic. Slobodan Kuruzovic is working as commander of the territorial defence staff of the Serbian army of the Prijedor Municipality. Alongside other duties, he has been active in Trnopolje from the very first day when the refugee centre was set up as the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor is well aware." Is this correct what we can read under number 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is correct. I am only not sure about the dates. I believe that I got this vehicle from this man earlier than that, but I'm not sure. Maybe five or six days earlier. I don't know exactly. All I know is that I asked for this vehicle to be accepted as mobilised but it was not done by the staff -- excuse me, by the logistics base. I registered this vehicle as a conscript's vehicle, as a vehicle that was mobilised by the secretariat of defence. I did it with Mr. Slavko Budimir. And as of that moment on, this vehicle became a soldier, just like I was a soldier. It was mobilised. When I was demobilised, I returned that vehicle, and I believe that that vehicle was then returned to its original owner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the assessment is correct, as we can read it here, "he, that is Slobodan Kuruzovic, has been active in Trnopolje from the very first day when the refugee centre was set up." It was not loud enough. Interpreters apparently couldn't hear you. You said "da," yes, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then the sentence starts: "Alongside many other duties, he has been active in Trnopolje." Could you please tell us which were these "many other duties"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is exactly that. The person who drafted this report tied things to the whole month preceding this report, because these certificates had to be issued. I don't know what else he had in mind. There were no other duties or tasks. As you can see, this is just a report of a person who wants to justify his work before his superiors and peppers it a little bit, as the popular saying goes. As far as my engagement in Trnopolje goes, this has been described correctly. I was there every day on a daily basis. And before the order was issued for me to be resubordinated to the brigade, before the decision was issued on the abolishment, I also looked after the vehicles, whether they were in good order, whether the food was being transported where it had to be transported. I checked the documents to avoid any abuse. I made sure that the food arrived and reached those that it was intended for. Because the times were, as I've already said, odd. I believe that I have already mentioned this. There were people who thought it was their right to do all sorts of things, without any authorisation, just because they wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then finally, coming back to the mere fact that you attended the meeting the 10th of June, 1992, and one of the enactments passed this day was the conclusion assigning the duty of providing security for the Trnopolje camp to the regional command. First of all, we should be aware that it reads here not "centre," not "reception centre," but "camp". And then why is it necessary if people are there, as you explained it until now, more or less on a voluntary basis, why is it necessary to provide security and then to the regional command bearing in mind the previous documents where the language was "camp," "prisoners," "prisoners of war"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you a little while ago with regard to the materiel and goods, this was the only way. Somebody had to be subordinated to somebody else. It was not the civilian police because it was not a prison. And there were lots more troops. And since I was subordinated to the army as of the 17th onwards, and even before that, the Crisis Staff and I asked for the army to provide security for these people because that was the safest way. There was a clear line of subordination. There were officers who were in charge of the 20 men-strong units. They would be there all night. They would return in the morning. They would be replaced by others, and they would report to the regional command that everything was carried out in order. If security had been provided by some private individuals serving as guards, all sorts of things might have happened. As it was, nothing did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now turn once again to the Prosecution. They tendered a document from -- dated Prijedor, the 30th of September, 1992. This would be provisionally marked S434A and B respectively. Please, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, before we leave the report on mobilised motor vehicles, just a few questions. Fikret Icic, would I be correct in assuming that he was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And now, if you turn to number 15 on the list of mobilised motor vehicles in the first part of the report, it indicates that on the 11th of May, 1992, a Zastava vehicle was mobilised and given to Vinko Kos of the SDS. I understand this to be a report that the only people that could mobilise vehicles were the army. Is that correct? It had to be under the authority of the army or the secretariat of national defence to mobilise a vehicle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vehicles were mobilised by the secretariat for national defence, and this vehicle was taken from the company Bosna Montaza, probably returned in good working order. Now why did Vinko from the SDS used it, I don't know. Maybe this person didn't know what this Vinko was doing. As far as I know, I believe that he was in a company, in a timber industry or somewhere. I don't know. I've forgot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Paragraph 13. Is this the same Vinko Kos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. He was in Lamovita in the sector staff. As far as I remember, he worked in a construction company. It's the same man. In one place, it says "sector staff"; in other place, it says the SDS. I don't know why this gentleman Mudrinic drafted it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, these are two different -- From the plate numbers given, these are two different vehicles. First let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you talk about the secretariat for national defence, you're speaking of the office headed by Mr. Budimir at this time, in the spring of 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. If these vehicles are mobilised for the purpose of the army, then a mobilisation chart has to be issued. It is possible that some of the vehicles were mobilised by the staff, not for the military Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. purposes, then a certificate would be issued and would be taken to the Executive Board, and it would be the secretary for the economy who would deal with that. And then the vehicles, such vehicles, would be returned to those that they were taken from. Those are -- were the vehicles which were mobilised for certain purposes and for no other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir. If we could now move to the next document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps Your Honour wants to mark this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's already marked provisionally S434A, B respectively. Prijedor, 30th of September 1992 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, looking at this document, it appears to be a report. It indicates in the introduction: Pursuant to the conclusion of the executive committee of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly of 5 May 1992, Dr. Srdjo Srdic is named as acting president of the Prijedor Red Cross. I'm summarising. You mentioned in your testimony to estimate the number of people who passed through the Trnopolje camp, and you told us you thought there were maybe six or seven thousand. Turning to page 9 of the English, I'll try to find it on the B/C/S, it's under Section 8 "conclusion and comment." I'm having trouble finding it on the B/C/S because the numbering of the sections does not make sense. On the B/C/S, I believe it's page 6954.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's number 13 in Roman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. It's number 13. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see, sir, that in the last point under that number 13, there are several indented paragraphs with a dash. The last one indicates that "23.000 people have been housed through the reception centre at Trnopolje, of whom we in the International Red Cross have dispatched 1.561 to the Karlovac reception centre. On 29 September, 1992, a convoy was escorted to Karlovac in the presence of European observers".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it would be appropriate also to read the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: "The problem of Trnopolje is becoming more complicated with the onset of autumn, so that there are those -- so that all those who have been left without homes are arriving in great numbers seeking accommodation. There are now more than 3.000 citizens there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, first, would it be correct that at times, the Trnopolje facility held up to 3.000 individuals?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. People came and went. There may have been even more. I never made any assessments or estimates.
