If this information was provided by the Red Cross, I don't know what they base their information on. Either on the number of people or on the number of meals, because a lot of these people were accommodated in the houses around. I cannot either confirm or dispute this Red Cross report. I don't think it is incorrect because I believe it was drafted in consultation with the International Red Cross and the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, how many different convoys were there to Croatia, not just Karlovac, but to Croatia from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any. There were organised departures from town, from Prijedor. And those were organised by the Red Cross. Maybe those people who left from town, they considered to have been in Trnopolje. This sounds a bit exaggerated to me. Maybe they did it on purpose for administrative reasons. I really don't know. I only know that very often, buses would leave from town. Whether they went off towards Croatia, I wouldn't know for a fact. You've already asked me, I believe it was the day before yesterday, about people having to pay their bills first, the utilities, and then they would leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, the Trnopolje facility was located a hundred, 200 metres from the railway station. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How many organised convoys were there from the Trnopolje facility using trains?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I believe two or three, possibly. I don't know. This was organised by the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly. Mr. Savanovic, I think, was the manager of the railroads, and he used the help of his colleagues in Zenica, and that's how people went. They were taken to Zenica. There were two or three-passenger vehicles at different time intervals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "passenger vehicles," the people were put on to cattle cars. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one of the convoys, in addition to passenger wagons, had two or three other ones, but there were more things there. It was hot. Not a single one of the convoys consisted merely of cattle cars. But I think there were freight cars that were included.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How many bus convoys were there out of the Trnopolje facility? Bus and truck convoys?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Well, I never kept any records on that. There were at least three or four, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that at one point, the convoys were going to Croatia, and then later they went to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any convoys going to Croatia. Central Bosnia, yes. That's why I'm saying, those who were going to Croatia, it's possible that they went by public transport organised by the Red Cross. They were going to Croatia. Except for what I mentioned about late 1991 and early 1992 when people were leaving the municipal territory with organised departures, mostly women, children, and the elderly, those who were men of military age and able-bodied men mostly remained in town. Now, what the reason was for that, I suppose they should know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We're breaking at 12.30, Your Honour? It may affect the order I do things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated -- let me ask you the following question: I'm going to ask you the same question I asked you in Banja Luka. Sir, in the times of conflict in Prijedor - I'm talking about May and June of 1992 - did the Crisis Staff and military work to coordinate their efforts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be difficult for me to answer that question. I don't believe that the Crisis Staff gave any orders to the army. As far as I can remember, the few meetings that I attended, two or three times there was Colonel Arsic or Zeljaja or Rajlic mainly with requests for meeting the needs of the army. If you actually meant that the Crisis Staff was ordering military operations, first of all, I don't remember any such thing. Secondly, I don't believe that that would have been possible. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, could you please be so kind and make reference to the page number of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm referring to page 46, line 10 of the transcript of our conversation in Banja Luka. And I will read again the question and the answer as it's translated -- transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: "In those times of the appeal and conflict in Prijedor, and I'm talking about May and June of 1992, did the Crisis Staff and military work to coordinate their efforts?" And you answered: "Yes." What did you mean? Do you deny that you answered yes to that question no Banja Luka, and if you do not deny it, would you like to explain your answer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I just have explained it. I don't mean to say there were no contacts between the civilian authorities and the military. But I assume that was your question, and that's perhaps why I said yes. It's not that the army didn't come to the Municipal Assembly, to the people in the leading positions because those were the people who were in a position to deal with the vital problems that the army was facing. So Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. accordingly, I do remember, although I was only there twice, perhaps three times, attending the meeting of the Crisis Staffs. And I know that they made certain requests at these meetings, but I can't remember any of the specifics, when, perhaps, the army had to go to the front, then lorries were to be secured because a lot of stuff had been destroyed. And what do I know? This is merely my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in fact, your own work at that time was an example of the coordination and the overlap between the civilian and military authorities. On Wednesday, on page 26, line 6 of Wednesday's transcript, you described yourself at that time as "I wasn't a soldier, I wasn't an army officer, I wasn't the Red Cross, and I was all that at one and the same time." So you were, yourself, both a municipal official, an army officer at the same time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it strikes me as a bit strange. I said it as a human being because there were great problems that we were facing. There was the camp at Trnopolje. Those people had to be taken care of. There were obligations related to the issuing of the vouchers and certificates. And then after about a fortnight, I received orders to join the army. So no wonder I referred to a number of different tasks and positions. I was not officially a member of the Red Cross, but, well, perhaps it's not a nice thing to say, but I took better care of those people over there than the Red Cross themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, were you -- you were tasked by the Crisis Staff to provide security at the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown S21, please. S21.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you have it yet? Sir, the usher is handing you S21 which indicates that at a meeting on the 6th of June, 1992, the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Prijedor issued the following conclusion: "The chief of the public security station, Simo Drljaca, and Slobodan Kuruzovic coordinate security of the Prijedor hospital. Which they will inform the Crisis Staff at the next meeting." Do you recall this meeting from the Crisis Staff, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the same thing, the one you've just given me. That's a different one. This is not the same document. This is on the blockade of the town, and then concerning the traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I gave you the wrong number. 71.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, this document also indicates that copies were given to the public security station, Simo Drljaca, Slobodan Kuruzovic, and the cashier Zarko Zgonjanin. Do you recall receiving this order or being present when it was made?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember neither. But there is some logic to such a thing being done, because that's one of the most sensitive facilities in the town. But I was in no way related to that as far as I remember, unless he actually -- unless this was represented as a decision, so probably they thought that someone from the barracks would do it. And in that case, I should be responsible, but I've never seen a conclusion like this one, although I do believe that this was a necessary step to be taken, for security to be provided for the hospital to prevent possible accidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Simo Drljaca about providing security at the hospital, or did you ever send -- arrange for any security for the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Not I. Whether I talked to him, I don't remember. But organised in cooperation with the public security centre, no, I didn't. I don't know how this -- why this includes my name, but here you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd now like to ask you some questions about the conditions and things that happened in the Trnopolje camp. You told us Wednesday on page 27 and 28, you were asked some questions -- you talked about people entering the camp and committing crimes, the last paragraph of page 27. You said: "On one occasion, some villagers, some local people entered, and I think some women, I believe four of them, were raped. Otherwise in that centre, there were physicians all the time. I think two physicians, two Muslims, and there were also nurses there. And in daytime, a doctor and a male nurse would come whenever it was necessary for them to do something. From what I know, people were taken to the hospital in Prijedor. Those rapes, to try to establish -- and I think only one of them was actually raped." Sir, how did you come to the conclusion that only one of the women was raped?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't come to any conclusion, but people talked over there. Those locals, because they were not inside any kind of fences. They were either outside in the street or at the Red Cross. They talked among themselves. I may have misheard, but I do know that those ladies, I'm not sure how old they were, they were taken to hospital. And now what was confirmed over there or not, and all the other things, I have no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that that one was the lady of an advanced age.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, how did you first learn that -- you originally said four women were raped by these villagers that came in. How did you first learn of this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came in the morning from the town, they told me that there had been such an incident, that the guards then intervened, and that doctors took care of those ladies and took them to hospital. That's what I found out when I came. But it was before the noon. It was not early in the morning. It was before the noon, and that's when I heard about that. I did not hear any of the details, though. The people from the Red Cross were talking about it because they had come before me and they said that women had been assailed. Well, that, and they referred to Cavic, but I don't know for sure. I don't know whether if it was that man or whether there was another man with him. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say "they told you" do you mean the people from the Red Cross, from the Serbian Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they, too, apparently heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What made you believe that only one of the women was raped, if you heard that they were -- the guards had intervened and four women had been raped?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether I referred or that one specially. I probably thought that because there was one woman who said something different. It wasn't a very decent thing to say. I wouldn't like to say it now. She said it was okay, that she wasn't -- and the rest she didn't know. But it seems that only one woman had sexual intercourse. I don't know about those others. The doctors' later official reports, I didn't get any official reports or anything. It was, you know, within the purview of the Red Cross, and they never told me anything about how the whole thing ended up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You never followed up to see what happened, who was arrested and what happened to the women?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I believe those women then came back to the open centre. Cavic was then arrested, and another man whose name escapes me now, another colleague who was there with them often. But how the whole thing ended, I don't know. I know that they were in prison. Now whether anyone else was taken away, I don't know. But I think that they told me the women actually went back to the centre and that they were fine. That's to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, didn't you tell us that Cavic was arrested for killing a policeman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at a later stage, much later actually, when the policeman was killed. That was a year later, more perhaps. I can't remember. Recently, something -- there was something about that in Kozarski Vjesnik remembering those people. But a long time has passed. That was after the centre at Trnopolje ceased to exist, maybe the next year. I don't know, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but there was only the police station then and they had a drunken brawl there, and then Cavic killed the police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, a few moments ago, I asked you how it was you determined it was one woman. You said it's ugly, but she said it was okay. Do you mean the woman who was raped said it was okay? Can you explain your comment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was told, that's what I heard. She was probably joking, because she is a very serious lady. Otherwise, how much at all, I think I heard they said thing about four women, but I don't know for sure, and I don't know what was ascertained at the hospital later and what the Red Cross reported about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, on page 35 of the interview in Banja Luka, beginning on line 10, you were talking about rapes in the camp. And you said: "Perhaps it's not nice to say it now because it's an ugly situation, but the older Muslims that were in there were also making jokes on that because we are that kind of people. How the older lady said that she had a nice time. It's not nice to say, but that's what I heard, like, two days after." So is that what you were repeating here, that you heard that the older woman indicated she had a nice time when she was raped?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, something along these lines, yes, what I said before, and now mainly I don't believe that. But yeah, that's how it was probably, some sort of a prank. I don't think anyone was seriously physically injured, otherwise people would have had a different reaction. You can't hide a thing like this from the people, because sooner or later, people learn about everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, could you please continue that we have it in the context the following lines of the statement on page 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Malik then asked you: "You mean the person who was raped, she said how nice it was?" And you answered: "Yes. Whether, she was raped now, but I don't know. Well anyway, there were no test results of any real defloration or any real defloration or anything because I just had other things to take care of in my mind. Those women later came to Trnopolje. No, I don't remember if it was one, two, or three. I don't remember exactly." I asked, "one, two, or three women?" And you said, "I'm not a man who lies, not even to my children or anyone else. I could have said that, I don't know, but I didn't hear. There were lots of stories about rapes, so if there was any, but not only in Trnopolje, but generally." And then you were asked by Mr. Malik, "what kinds of stories about rapes?" And you said, "stories you would read about all over the country, in newspapers all over the country that happened, regardless of whether it's Muslims to Serbs, Serbs to Muslims, or Croats to other two." Mr. Malik asked: "In fact, isn't it true that girls as young as 12, 13, and 14 were being raped in Trnopolje? You answered: "I never heard about that, except it's possible that the Muslims did that to themselves because there were many young people of both sexes, and perhaps later it has been said that it was something else. But as much as I know, the army did not go in there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, when you talk about stories all over the country, isn't it true that there was a lot of publicity in Prijedor about Serbian women being raped in camps in places like Bosanski Brod, in Celebici, in Dretelj, which a Croat-HVO camp that one of our witnesses Mr. Vulliamy visited. And that there was a lot of publicity about what was being done to Serbian women around Bosnia by Muslim and Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you're right, and vice versa. The publicity, these are things that one should not keep silent about, no matter who the people in question are. The other side said the same. And the third side said the same. They still speak about it and I don't think one should stop speaking about these things. Military activity is one thing, and this is an altogether different thing. I am sorry that I was not fully informed about all these things, how many women and whatever. As for this statement of yours, yes, you are right. And this goes for all the different ethnic groups and for all the information, and for all the reports and for all the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, at the camp during the night, you had young army recruits guarding the camp. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't looking at their age, but there were few young people there. Mostly elderly, from town. Elderly people from town, many people knew each other. The Muslims and those who were the guards then, but yeah, it's possible there were young people there, too. I was not considering their age.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: These men that were guarding the camp, whether they were younger or older, they had heard these stories. They had also heard the statement in Kozarski Vjesnik and the media that the Muslims had a plan to commit genocide on the Serbs. And they were indoctrinated by these reports to fear and to hate the Muslims. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are difficult questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Asks for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objection dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are jumping at conclusions, jumping to conclusions. I think you're saying this was indoctrination, and just because those people were actually watching TV and this was an act of revenge and that they were trying to get back on the others, this is not something I find myself inclined to believe. Because this is not what happened in Prijedor at the time. Then on the other hand, you could expect, for example, that in the centre at Trnopolje or down there in town, on a massive scale, hundreds of them, this would have been psychological pressure, indoctrination, but nothing like that ever occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, most of the people in the Trnopolje camp were women and children. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one period, yes; at one period, no. In the camp, in the open centre, not the camp, the open centre, there were women there, children, elderly people, young people, depending on the period of time. Sometimes those prevailed and sometimes the other group prevailed. There were young people there, too, Muslims and, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There were young women there, young girls. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as long as women were there, that means there would have been young and somewhat older children, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt at this moment, but could you please explain what you just said on page 59, line 19: You made a distinction between in the camp, in the open centre, not the camp. Could you please explain the distinction between Trnopolje camp and the open centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was convinced that I have already explained this on several occasions. You've noticed that in this report, this logistics man from the logistics base says a refugee centre. This -- or shelter. This is a word used in our area which means "to take refuge from a problem," to take shelter. That's why it's not a camp. A camp is a place where people are being brought in an organised fashion, such as in World War II, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. They were your own words. "In the camp, in the open centre, not the camp. The open centre, there were women there, children, elderly people." So when was you making now the distinction now between the open centre and the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. I addressed Mr. Koumjian, and I told him not to use the word "camp." That's why I've repeated it several times. Normally, I never use this word. But the whole thing altogether, it was called the open centre. There were no particular sections. And it really was open. It remained open the whole time. You can translate it as "open centre." But our people, not the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serbs only, but all the people over there, they refer to these places as shelters, a place where people take shelter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Koumjian, do you want to continue now or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll just ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, what did you do to protect the women and girls in Trnopolje from being raped?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was nothing special I could do, except all those people who were bringing their own security units over there, I warned them against entering the school building if possible, the warehouse that was there, the storage where people were being kept in order to keep strange things from happening. And this was a successful measure, nothing ever happened except that once. I warned them to stay outside to keep the same things from happening. When those people came from Petrov Gaj, those paramilitaries, and do stupid things. Not only these serious things, but I wanted to make sure no contact was possible between the locals and those people coming in and wreaking havoc. That was the only thing I was in a position to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And did you yourself set an example for gentlemanly behaviour towards the women in the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly hope so. I don't recall any complaints. A delegation came once, an international delegation containing a congressman. He asked me to meet me specially to tell me that he had heard everyone was happy there with my behaviour and my treatment of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This is an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 2.00 sharp. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if anyone's in the public gallery now. Could we begin in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think to be on the safe side, we have -- it's your intention to play a video now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask a few questions, but related to the witness from the video before I play it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think then to be on the safe side, we have to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are already in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, the video that you saw, you saw the young man whose back was covered, his whole body, with black and blue marks. Did you see men like that, boys like that in the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the open centre Trnopolje, I never saw anybody like that. I remember when those people came, a C group from Omarska, that's what they called them, I believe. Some of them were a bit thin. I never saw anybody injured, nor did anybody tell me about that. People would have told me because a lot of these people knew me and they would have complained to me. And a number of them were really glad to find me there because they knew me and they knew that there wouldn't be any problems because we helped them there to recover. There was just one person who was sick. I believe his nickname or his family name was Hadzalija. He was brought on a stretcher because he was ill, and he was seen by a doctor that we provided for him, and he also was glad to see me. Some six months ago, he died in Prijedor. He had returned to Prijedor. He had lived there with his family, and I would see him very often. Sometimes we would play preference, a card game together. And I saw that picture with -- depicting that person with scars and marks, but I never saw any such person in Trnopolje. Believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You saw on the video a young doctor, Idriz Merdzanic. Do you recall him being in the camp -- excuse me, in the open reception centre of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That is the name -- the man whose name I didn't know when you talked to me. I believe that he was an amateur pilot, a sports pilot. There was him and another doctor, and a male nurse and two female nurses or maybe one. I can't remember exactly. In addition to this doctor and the male nurse, who would come from Prijedor -- again I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was Dr. Merdzanic and the other doctor, who I believe you know as Jusuf Pasic --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Pasic, correct. I don't know his name. I didn't know about the other guy, that his name was Merdzanic. I forgot. And there was also this guy Pasic, together with him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were they free to leave the camp whenever they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they went to Prijedor. I don't know which one of them and when they went. I believe they went to fetch some medicines from the surgery in Kozarac, and they brought some drugs and some dressing and other things. I don't know when that was, but I know that they went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So Dr. Merdzanic was another one of the refugees that you assisted in the open reception centre at Trnopolje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would he have any reason to mislead this Court about the conditions under which he was there and the fact that he says he was not free to leave?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. What do I know? Again, there may be God knows what agenda behind that. He didn't want to leave. I understood that he was from Kozarac, and if he was to go to Prijedor, he would have had to stay with somebody, or maybe he would have been attacked by somebody. But I never heard it from him that he wanted to leave and was not allowed to leave. Why does he now want to state differently I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Actually, Dr. Merdzanic was from Prijedor but was caught in Kozarac during the attack during the one day of the week that he held a clinic there. Dr. Jusuf Pasic was taken from Trnopolje and taken to Omarska and killed. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honest to God, I don't know that. I believe that once the police came, and they took him for an interview. Where he was taken to, I don't know. I heard it only subsequently. I heard that he was taken to Omarska. And what his lot was, I don't know. I didn't know about Merdzanic, that he was from Prijedor and that he was forced to come to Trnopolje from Kozarac. As far as I remember, the majority of the people there came of their own will. When I arrived there, people were already there. And after that, they kept coming and coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And they would -- many of them came in buses escorted by police and army. Correct? For example, in the late July, when the Brdo area was cleansed, buses arrived carrying men from Brdo. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, men and women with their families. But that was to remove them from the area where combat activities were taking place. Yes, now you've reminded me. I believe there were either one or two buses, but I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you told that those buses came to Trnopolje because Omarska was full?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How am I to remember that, I really don't know. According to what I heard and according to what was going on in Omarska, I heard that there were investigations, there were judges there, that there were interrogations going on. That has nothing whatsoever to do with Trnopolje, it's a totally different thing. So now I don't know what you mean when you say there was no place in Omarska. People who took refuge from combat activities came to Trnopolje. As for the others and for what grounds they were taken elsewhere, I don't know. Maybe they have killed somebody or something else. I really don't know why people were taken to other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown by the Judge S12 which was a certificate signed by you and Pero Curguz indicating that someone had the authority to leave the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And on page 40 of Friday's transcript, Mr. Lukic was asking you about the fact that people had to get approval, even Serbs, from the Ministry of Defence to leave the territory or the secretariat for national defence. Sir, you were not a representative of the Ministry of Defence or secretariat for national defence, were you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. A conscript had to get an approval to be able to leave town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Because it was during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Since neither you or Mr. Curguz knew or had records of people's mobilisation or military service, then why was it that you and Mr. Curguz signed this certificate allowing this person to leave Trnopolje and the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't a clue to be honest. I really don't remember this document. I saw it here. It was sitting in front of me. I saw that Pero signed it. I saw the number and the Autonomous Region of Krajina, but I really don't know what this could have referred to. Maybe it could have been something along these lines, people were filling out when they arrived there. Then the Red Cross representatives had to take the personal details of these people according to the Geneva Conventions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Maybe I have signed such a blank form. Maybe not one but even more of them. And maybe these blank forms were to be filled in at a later date, and maybe somebody abused that. I'm not saying that for a fact. I'm not allowed to say something that is not correct. But I really don't know what this is all about, who these people are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: For the purpose -- for the benefit of counsel for the Defence and for Your Honours, I'm referring to page 9518 of the testimony, prior transcript of Witness DD.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in order for someone to be released from the Trnopolje reception centre, did they have to get a guarantee from a Serb? Did you ever hear about that procedure, where Serbs had to give a guarantee to have friends or relatives released from the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember ever having seen or heard anything like that. I only know that there were some officers who came for their families or relatives. There was a JNA officer who was a Muslim who came to fetch his family, and then these families could be certain that nothing would happen to them. But as for those guarantees, that you mentioned I don't remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, would members of the intervention squad bring people to the camp, to Trnopolje? Excuse me. Let me rephrase the question. Did you see members of the intervention squad bringing people to the Trnopolje reception centre, the intervention squad of the Prijedor police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I know that there was fighting at one point, and that was in Kozarac. And people who lived in Suvi Brod close to the road, maybe two families came, and they said there were some specials up there. But nobody of that sort brought people to Trnopolje. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you, sir, give permission to a group of people to go or instructions to go bury a family that was killed close to the camp, the Foric family?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such thing. I don't know that family. That may have been somebody from the Red Cross. I don't remember -- I remember one Foric. He was the trade union representative in town, or a member of the socialist union. He was a young, very, very nice man. But I don't remember this particular incident. Nothing similar to that happened in the centre. Maybe it was something that happened far away from the centre, but then it would have been the Red Cross who would have dealt with that, not me. I don't remember anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This would be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until half past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue. Sorry for the delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'll try to ask direct questions, and if you keep your answers short, hopefully we can finish this afternoon. You indicated you're not sure whether you were present when the foreign journalists first came to the camp. Sir, I'm putting it to you that the foreign journalists that made the video that you saw, Penny Marshall, Ed Vulliamy, and Mr. Williams, came on the 5th of August. Isn't it true that following that visit, there then were a great number of journalists from all over the world coming to Prijedor and to the Trnopolje camp to report on what was happening in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether this was the first visit, but if you say so, I'm sure you're right. Many journalists came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that the International Red Cross, as opposed to the local Red Cross, which was headed by Srdjo Srdic, the International Red Cross did not have access to the Trnopolje camp until after the foreign journalists had visited the camp in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this was the case. I believe that they came much earlier, both them and the -- as well as the UNHCR. I can't claim that to be a fact, but I believe that they came much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, you would certainly know when the International Red Cross showed up at the Trnopolje centre, I would assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit S238, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that the authorities in Prijedor and the Crisis Staff had denied the International Red Cross access to the camp until the foreign journalists came there on the 5th of August and after the reporting in the world press?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. If I said something, I don't know. I would be lying. It is possible, but I don't recall those events in any particular sequence. I don't remember the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And Ms. Karper has another document to be distributed now. Sir, going to Exhibit S238, I'm going to read to you the last sentence which is a quote from Predrag Radic, the mayor of Banja Luka, following a visit of officials from Banja Luka to the camp -- excuse me, to Prijedor. And it indicates "to the collection centres." Mr. Radic is quoted as saying, in the last sentence: "The International Red Cross has been trying for days to reach Prijedor, but as we have stated, we will make it possible for them only after they personally acknowledge the situation of Serbian refugees and captives in Odzak, Rascani, Travnik, Zenica, Sarajevo, Konjic, and many other places." Now, sir I'd also like you -- there's another document which we have only in English which I will read to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And Your Honour, this bears the ERN number 00317985.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be provisionally marked D435A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This is dated, sir, this is a press release, the 2nd of October, 1992. "ICRC evacuates 1.560 people from Trnopolje camp." Paragraph it indicates on the first sentence: "The International Committee of the Red Cross confirmation having evacuated on 1st of October 1.560 people from Trnopolje camp near Prijedor in northwestern Bosnia-Herzegovina to a reception centre in Karlovac southwest of Zagreb where they were handed over to staff of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees. The evacuation started in the early morning and was completed during the night. The people concerned are civilian victims of the ongoing hostilities in northern Bosnia and had all been visited and provided with assistance by ICRC delegates since the ICRC was first able to enter the camp on 10 August." Sir, reminding you that you are under oath, isn't it a fact that the International Red Cross was not permitted into the camp, did not come to the camp until after the foreign journalists' visit in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Again, you've taken me by surprise with these dates, like the Defence counsel before you. I don't remember that it was so late, unless it was something unofficial. This now shows me again -- because it was not just the UNHCR and the Red Cross from Prijedor that came, but also representatives of the International Red Cross, and I don't believe that it happened as late as you claim it did. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you explain, sir, why Predrag Radic would say that we're not going to allow the ICRC to reach Prijedor until camps that Serbs are held in are first inspected?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He was a political leader in Banja Luka. I don't remember what he was exactly. I think he was a mayor. I don't know what he was before that, so I cannot provide any comment about his words. I don't think that he could impose any conditions. What the Red Cross is doing has nothing whatsoever to do with politics or fighting. He should have allowed them because what the Red Cross is doing is providing better conditions for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you explain why the Red Cross press release would indicate that they were first able to enter the camp on the 10th of August?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again camp, okay, very well then. This means that officially, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they were not allowed. I don't think that I've gotten that old and forgetful. Maybe this was official because Mr. Mignon came at that time, and I believe that he held some talks there. I believe that the president of the Executive Board was also there. I did not participate in those talks. I did not voice any opinions because that was outside of the scope of my authorities and competencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, the visit by Mr. Mignon that you're speaking of, he said that he spoke to others that are outside your authority. Who did he speak to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Dr. Mico Kovacevic, the president of the Executive Board was there, as well as representatives of the Red Cross. Later on, I heard that he was angry that the International Red Cross wanted to organise their transportation. I believe that I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that the persons in the Trnopolje reception centre were not registered by the Red Cross until after the 21st of August, in other words, that they were not registered yet when the convoy set off for Vlasic mountain in which over 200 men were killed at Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the registers were open much earlier. I'm not sure, but this is what I believe. I've forgotten. It was a long time ago. However, I believe that it was much earlier. I remember there was a woman whose name was Angie. She was an interpreter. I remember her sitting under a tree and writing something down together with those people from the Red Cross. I believe that this must have been earlier on, but I don't know it for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to read to you from the testimony of Dr. Idriz Merdzanic. It's page 7789 of the trial transcript. He was asked: "I want to ask you about one particular convoy about which you later heard that the people had been killed. Did you see the loading of the people that eventually you heard from killed on Mount Vlasic?" And Dr. Merdzanic answered: "That was, I think, the last convoy to leave Trnopolje, and that was when the International Red Cross had already announced their arrival. I think in fact that the representatives of the International Red Cross had already arrived in Trnopolje, but the camp inmates had not been registered yet. So over the next two days, this convoy was organised, which could be joined freely by men, whoever could fit on to the lorries and buses. Up to that point, it was only on rare occasions that any of the men managed to smuggle themselves out, but this time, they could join." Does this remind you that in fact the International Red Cross had not yet taken down the names of the men that were put on the convoy over Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. According to what you say, that is a possibility. Still, I'm convinced that it was earlier on and Dr. Merdzanic must have made a mistake. As far as I know, after that, there were one or two more transportations for people. I believe that every time, there were one or two buses leaving, and nothing happened to these people. Now, I'm so confused that I really can't remember things clearly. I believe that there were more --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you were present that day at Trnopolje when the buses and trucks were loaded, the men that went over Mount Vlasic on the convoy where the massacre occurred at Koricanske Stijene, and you also were present that day in Tukovi when the trucks were loaded of persons wanting to join the convoy from a separate origin at Tukovi. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't believe that those were only men. It never happened that it would be only men leaving. Most often, it would be families, women and children leaving. And as for Tukovi, yes, I was asked to go down there by the Red Cross because these people down there only trusted me, and nobody else. Some of them even asked me to influence these people not to leave because by that time, the incidents had stopped in town and Trnopolje was very safe. It was the safest place in town, because there were no killings or looting there. Nobody could take anybody away from there. Some people whom I know, for example, Mehto [phoen] who has returned to Prijedor and some others who lived there whom I've seen several times, and I saw his wife and I was asked to influence those people not to leave. Later on, it turned out that some people, members of my people for material gain have destroyed people's lives. And I'm sure that my people, my town, will be ashamed because of them for as long as they live. Because before that, nothing of that sort had ever happened. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that Prijedor was safe at that time. In fact, it was safe because after the foreign journalists came and world attention focussed on Prijedor, the Omarska camp, the Keraterm camp were closed, and the killing had stopped inside the municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honest to God, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who organised the buses, the trucks, the fuel and drivers for those buses and trucks, and the security for that convoy on the 21st of August over Vlasic mountain?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the equipment was concerned, the materiel organisation, it was the Executive Board, Dr. Mico Kovacevic. As for the security, it was the public security centre or rather the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who was present providing the security on those buses? Who did you see at the Trnopolje camp and at Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at Tukovi, I didn't see anyone providing security. As far as Trnopolje, I really don't remember. Do you remember when we talked last year around the same time, those people were too young. I didn't know those people. Except now I heard that Mrdja had been arrested and brought to The Hague and he, too, had been escorting that particular convoy. Other than that, I don't remember those people. I was already 50 at that time, plus everything I had to go through, and the death of my daughter. I just wasn't paying attention. The only thing I really tried to do was to look after those people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you describe what Dado Mrdja looked like at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was a long time ago. I know what he's like. He's rather tall, dark hair. He was probably wearing uniform, if he was escorting. Then he must have been wearing police uniform. I believe he was wearing glasses for a while, but I can't really remember that. A small man whom they called Babin, also an ex-student of mine, was also escorting one of those convoys. But Dado, I don't remember his being there. And this other man, I did see him once because he gave me a jacket once when they set out. I think he's in a wheelchair now. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is that Zoran Babic, nicknamed Babin or Bakin?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's possible. I've forgotten, but that sounds possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that Babin and Dado Mrdja were in the same unit, that you would see them together?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, it's possible that they were. But I don't remember seeing them. They were the police. I didn't have anything special to do with them. Whether they were together then or not, I don't know. But I do remember that the small man brought me an apple. But I can't remember seeing Dado there, and I didn't even know the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You worked every day with Pero Curguz. Do you know the name of his son?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honest to God, I can't remember. But, yes, I do know his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is that Igor Curguz?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Igor, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was he a member of the police, the same unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think so. He was a student at the time in Banja Luka, I believe. He was pursuing his studies, and he only came to Prijedor occasionally, because Pero over there and me and there was his son and I don't know. I'm not sure if he was a member of that police unit or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you know Dado Mrdja when you were fighting in Croatia? Did Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you see him there in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that either. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a document, draft translation L0099217. And the B/C/S is 01190801. It's a response to a request for assistance to the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be provisionally marked S436A and B respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, this short document, as you can see, is a response to an inquiry regarding the service of Darko Mrdja. If you turn to the bottom, look at the bottom of that document, the second page of the English, would it be correct that Mr. Mrdja was in the army, served in the military, from September 19th, 1991, until April 29th, 1992, at which time he was then transferred to the police. And he was in the police until September the 9th, 1992, and then transferred back to the military. Can you tell us whether you find it significant or could explain why it was that someone would be transferred on the 29th of April from the military to the police? That would be the night before the takeover.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It may be that this indicates that there is a coincidence between these dates, but this is regular work for the Ministry of Defence. I see this is signed by Aleksic. I'm not sure. I can't comment on this. I don't know what it has to do with these dates. All I can see is he was transferred from the army to the police and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that people were mentioned the name of Dado Mrdja as being one of the perpetrators of the massacre immediately following the massacre, in the next few days?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never heard his name or the name of any of the others. I did hear that, well, since we knew that the police was escorting, that this had happened. Now, whether they all participated in it, whether everyone was shooting those people over there, were they all perpetrators of this crime, I don't know. I don't even know if it was on that day, what I said about that young man once when he was escorting that people, he gave me that. Once, it was on a train, I believe. But I can't be sure really, the apple. At which time, which buses, I'm sorry really I don't know who meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, how is it that you mentioned you wrote a report and you learned about this two or three days after the massacre. How is it that you could not at that time remember the name of any of the people providing the escorts to the convoy? Is that what you're saying, that you did not at that time remember the name of any of the escorts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time, not now. Here, I know these names here, but I'm not sure these people were actually there then. I assume you are in a situation to check the statement. I don't even know myself how courts work. But in that statement, I didn't say who was there or who led them. They asked me to say on which day this happened, the transport was organised by the Autotransport Company through the Executive Board, and that security was provided by the public security centre. That was all I was asked to say in that statement. As for the other things that happened, I'm really sorry, I don't know, as for the other people. I did hear a lot of other things later on TV and so on and so forth at that time. For two days maybe, I heard about it, I think, that's unless I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, who would have had the record -- first, there were more than a thousand people probably in that convoy, correct, between the buses, the trucks in Tukovi, and the buses that came to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe it was that many. But there were quite a number, yes. You mean who might have the record as to who the people were who had joined the convoy, or who escorted the convoy? Now, as to who escorted them, that should still be at the public security centre, I suppose. I don't believe they just went like that without anyone knowing. That would have been impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How many police would have escorted a convoy of that size?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, there was always one police officer with a driver in the bus. And that's how they provided security for those people when travelling. I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So there would have been one police escort on each of the vehicles, and there also would have been at least one police car leading the way. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct. That's one thing I forgot. There was a police vehicle, yes, excuse me. You see, I keep forgetting things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If a convoy left from Trnopolje and Tukovi, went to Travnik or the front line at Smetovi and returned in one day, at that time that would have been -- that would have taken all day, correct, that journey there and back?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once back, the buses would go back to Autotransport. They were not reporting to me. So I don't know what exactly happened, but sometimes they would just phone me and tell me that they reached Travnik without any trouble and down at Trnopolje, the Red Cross, many people would call.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So, sir, it would have been relatively easy to obtain the police records of who was escorting the convoy on that all-day journey. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. If you went looking for those at the public security centre, well, probably. But this should have been done by the Executive Board. The order should have come from them to whoever was the organiser of those convoys, that is, the president of the Executive Board. I was only looking after the people, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, the Executive Board followed the instructions or served under the Municipal Assembly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Municipal Assembly was the legislative power, and the Executive Board was the executive power. And all jobs, no matter what the area, there would always be someone on the Executive Board appointed for those jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that the top political position in the municipality was president of the Municipal Assembly as seen by the fact that Professor Cehajic was given that position when the SDA won the most seats in the 1990 election?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And later, Stakic took up that position. That's the highest legislative authority, or rather the highest representative of legislative authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The highest political position, the position seen by the people of Prijedor as being the top political representative of the people in the municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence, do you have any questions in return?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would probably have only to clarify the functions of the president of the municipality, but I think that this witness already answered that he does not know what the functions of the bodies in the municipality are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you would have no further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If Your Honours do not have any questions, I might finish in two, three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please. Further questions by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kuruzovic, just -- this will not take more than two minutes. Do you know which are the duties of the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe we've answered this once already. He carries out the decisions of the Municipal Assembly. If the Municipal Assembly adopts a decision, that's actual -- actually, he doesn't carry them out, he signs them. But if these are implemented, then this is supposed to be done by the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly. At least that's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if any of the members of the Executive Board are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. responsible to the president of the Municipal Assembly? Do they answer to the president of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they answer to the assembly, not to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, the position of the president of the Municipal Assembly, was it more representational in character, or does it have any real actual power?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably the former, it's more ceremonial. That's the case with most presidents, when the assemblies meet, they preside over the sessions. But the true executive power lies with the Executive Board, and they report in writing to the assembly on their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Kuruzovic. I've no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Anybody else, any question? This is not the case. Then we have to discuss the admission into evidence of the documents tendered today. S432, 17th of August. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position is that each and single document offered today in which the Crisis Staff is mentioned is late to be asked for the admission. So the OTP had the obligation to disclose to us all the documents dealing with the Prijedor Crisis Staff. And obviously, it has not been done until today. So yes, we object on these grounds, among others, to S432.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this is a general remark related to all the documents from S432 through S436. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just checking whether the Crisis Staff is mentioned in every and single one. S435 does not have mentioned the name of the Crisis Staff, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S435. Any other objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only there is no source for this document, for S435, there is no source. This is -- it's not known who composed the document or to whom it was sent. And the last one, S436, we do not have any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear the submission by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe that none of these fall under Rule 68. We're not obligated to disclose them. They all were in direct response to the testimony of this witness. Two of the documents counsel mentioned were previously disclosed in any event, and they are S432, which was disclosed on the 65 ter list as 316; and S434, which was disclosed on the 65 ter list as 368. As for the source of the ICRC, we could have Mr. Inayat add that to his sourcing list, which is actually -- he has prepared it except for these new documents, and we could submit that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be correct to regard this as an official press release.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It is a press release. It's a public document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be in the public domain and no doubt be accessible even on the internet. But let's wait one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: All the documents mentioned are under the respective numbers admitted into evidence. It is true that S432 and S434 were already 65 ter as 316 and 368. Document S433 was apparently not 65 terred, but it was a response, a clear response, to the question which Crisis Staff meetings Mr. Kuruzovic attended, especially the one of the 10th of June, 1992, and also on the question of the mobilisation of one or several cars. Then 435A, public domain. 436, nothing is mentioned about the Crisis Staff. It's only apparently related to this case that Mr. Mrdja seems, as it's written here, to have left the military post the 29th of April, 1992, and this would be a question of the evaluation of evidence. So therefore, these are the reasons why we decided to admit these documents into evidence. Mr. Kuruzovic, this was a very long testimony of yours. It was -- whatever the content was, it was extremely difficult for you. Therefore, do you want to add anything from your side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only thank you. But yes, if I may, I would like to add a sentence or two. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Please in --
